title: Review: Kinematics; Forces and momentum
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: A.2#c36 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; A.2#c27 bank term, clue written for the game from the bank's definition; A.1.7#xt1 term and clue written for the game; A.1.9#xt2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: A.1#q11, A.1#q15, A.1#q18, A.2#q02, A.2#q04, A.2#q06, A.1#q12, A.1#q13, A.1#q20, A.2#q03, A.2#q05, A.2#q33. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Time period, T
items.clue: How long one complete revolution takes.

items.label: Elastic collision
items.clue: Total kinetic energy is the same before and after.

items.label: Acceleration
items.clue: The rate of change of velocity; the gradient of a velocity–time graph.

items.label: Terminal speed
items.clue: The constant value reached by a falling body once the drag on it balances its weight.

questions.stem: A car starts from rest and moves along a straight road. Its acceleration is greatest at the start and decreases continuously, falling quickly at first and then more slowly, but stays positive, until the car reaches 20 m s⁻¹ at t = 10 s. Which gives the distance travelled by the car in these 10 s?

options.text: Between 100 m and 200 m, since its speed rises fastest early on
Exactly 100 m, as its average velocity is (0 + 20)/2 m s⁻¹
Exactly 200 m, as it moves at 20 m s⁻¹ for the whole 10 s
Less than 100 m, as the curve of its velocity–time graph bends upwards

questions.explanation: The velocity–time graph rises steeply and then flattens, so it lies above the straight line from (0, 0) to (10 s, 20 m s⁻¹), whose area is 100 m. The velocity stays below 20 m s⁻¹ until t = 10 s, so the area is also less than 20 × 10 = 200 m.

questions.stem: A stone is thrown from the top of a cliff at 15.0 m s⁻¹ at 30.0° below the horizontal. It lands in the sea 40.0 m below the point of release. Fluid resistance is negligible. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². How long after release does the stone reach the sea?
questions.explanation: The initial vertical velocity is 15.0 sin 30.0° = 7.50 m s⁻¹ downwards. With downwards positive, 40.0 = 7.50t + 4.9t², whose positive root is t = 2.19 s.

questions.stem: A small steel ball is released from rest in air and falls until it reaches terminal speed. How does its acceleration change during this time?

options.text: It is constant but less than g, because fluid resistance is constant.
It stays equal to g, since fluid resistance only lowers the ball's speed.
It increases, since the ball moves faster and faster as it falls.
It decreases from g towards zero as the fluid resistance increases.

questions.explanation: At release the ball is at rest, so there is no fluid resistance and its acceleration is g. As it speeds up the fluid resistance grows, so its acceleration decreases, reaching zero at terminal speed.

questions.stem: A book rests on a horizontal table. The weight of the book is the gravitational force exerted on it by the Earth. Which force forms a Newton's third law pair with this weight?

options.text: The normal force exerted on the book by the table
The contact force exerted on the table by the book
The gravitational force exerted on the Earth by the book
No force, because the book is too small to pull the Earth

questions.explanation: A third-law pair is the two forces of ONE interaction, here the gravitational interaction between the book and the Earth. The Earth pulls the book down; the book pulls the Earth up with a force of equal magnitude. The two forces are of the same type and act on different bodies.

questions.stem: A ball is thrown vertically upwards. Air resistance is negligible. Which force or forces act on the ball while it is still rising, after it has left the hand?

options.text: Its weight and a decreasing upward force from the throw
Its weight and an upward force larger than its weight
No force until it stops at the top and then starts to fall
Only its weight, the downward pull of the Earth

questions.explanation: Once the ball leaves the hand, the only body still interacting with it is the Earth (air resistance is negligible). Its weight acts downwards throughout the flight, which is why the ball slows as it rises.

questions.stem: A box is pulled at constant velocity across a rough horizontal floor by a rope that makes an angle of 30° above the horizontal. Which list gives all the forces that should appear on a free-body diagram of the box, and no others?

options.text: Weight, normal force, tension, friction, push of box on floor
Weight, normal force, tension, friction, forward force of motion
Weight, normal force, rope tension and friction from the floor
Weight, tension and friction; the rigid floor exerts no push up

questions.explanation: A free-body diagram shows every force that other bodies exert ON the box: the Earth (weight F_g), the floor (normal force F_N and friction F_f) and the rope (tension T). Nothing else touches the box or exerts a field force on it.

questions.stem: A graph of velocity against time for a sprinter starts at the origin, rises steeply, becomes gradually less steep, and is a horizontal line at 11 m s⁻¹ from t = 6.0 s until the end of the race. Which describes the sprinter's motion?

options.text: The acceleration decreases, so the sprinter is slowing down after the start.
The acceleration increases, since the sprinter keeps getting faster.
The acceleration falls to zero, and the sprinter is at rest after 6.0 s.
The acceleration falls to zero while the speed rises to a steady value.

questions.explanation: The gradient of a velocity–time graph is the acceleration. The gradient decreases from a large value to zero at t = 6.0 s, while the height, the velocity, rises to 11 m s⁻¹ and then stays constant.

questions.stem: A ball is kicked horizontally at 12 m s⁻¹ from the top of a vertical cliff 20 m high and lands on level ground below. Fluid resistance is negligible. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². How far from the foot of the cliff does the ball land?
questions.explanation: Vertically, the ball starts with zero vertical velocity: 20 = ½ × 9.8 × t², so t = 2.02 s. Horizontally, its velocity stays 12 m s⁻¹, so it travels 12 × 2.02 = 24 m.

questions.stem: A small plastic ball is launched without spin from level ground at 30° above the horizontal. The motion is compared with an identical launch in which fluid resistance is negligible. Which describes the effect of fluid resistance on the ball's motion?

options.text: The range is shorter, and the horizontal velocity component decreases during the flight.
The range is shorter, but the horizontal velocity component stays constant in flight.
The range is shorter, and the highest point is still reached at exactly half the range.
The range is unchanged, as the ball follows the same path but moves more slowly.

questions.stem: A lamp of mass 5.0 kg hangs at rest, supported by two cables, one on each side. Each cable makes an angle of 40° with the horizontal, and the arrangement is symmetrical. Take g = 9.8 m s⁻². What is the tension in each cable?
questions.explanation: The lamp is in translational equilibrium, so the resultant force is zero. The horizontal components of the tensions cancel. Vertically, 2T sin 40° = mg, so T = (5.0 × 9.8 N)/(2 × 0.643) = 38 N.

questions.stem: A car of mass 1.2 × 10³ kg travelling at 20 m s⁻¹ collides head-on with a truck of mass 1.2 × 10⁴ kg travelling at 10 m s⁻¹. How does the force exerted by the truck on the car compare with the force exerted by the car on the truck during the collision?

options.text: The truck's force is larger, since the truck has more mass.
They are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
The car's force is larger, since the car is moving faster.
The truck's force is larger, since the car's velocity changes more.

questions.explanation: The two forces are the two sides of one interaction between the car and the truck, so by Newton's third law they are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, whatever the masses and speeds.

questions.stem: A person stands on the floor of a lift that is accelerating upwards. Which description of a correct free-body diagram for the person is right?

options.text: Two arrows: the weight downwards and a normal force of equal size from the floor upwards.
Two arrows: the weight downwards and a larger normal force from the floor upwards.
Three arrows: the weight, the normal force, and an upward force of the lift's motion.
Three arrows: the weight, the normal force, and the person's push down on the floor.
